q.s: A 68-year-old man has fatigue and exertional dyspnea for 3 months. He takes no medications and eats a normal diet. He has conjunctival pallor. Stool guaiac testing is positive. His laboratory results are shown.
o: Start oral iron and recheck in 1 year
e: Wrong. The cause must be found.
Wrong. Iron studies already explain the anemia.
Wrong. Not needed with clear iron deficiency.
Correct. Iron deficiency in an older man with positive stool blood needs evaluation for colorectal cancer.
cl: In older men, iron deficiency means GI blood loss until proven otherwise.
q.ch: Older man + microcytic anemia + low iron, high TIBC, low ferritin, high RDW (table) + occult blood → iron deficiency from GI loss → colonoscopy.
q.tr: Low ferritin is the most specific test for iron deficiency.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

q.s: A 24-year-old woman of Italian descent has mild microcytic anemia found on routine testing. She feels well and has normal menstrual periods. Her laboratory results are shown.
e: Correct. β-thalassemia minor: Mentzer index 63/6.0 ≈ 10.5 (<13), high RBC count, elevated HbA2; no treatment needed.
Wrong. Ferritin is normal; iron may cause overload.
cl: No obvious cause of iron loss.
q.ch: Mediterranean + mild microcytosis + high RBC count + Mentzer <13 + normal ferritin + high HbA2 (table) → β-thalassemia minor → reassurance.
q.tr: Mentzer index (MCV/RBC) <13 = thalassemia trait; >13 = iron deficiency.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

q.s: A 22-year-old African American man has had one episode of painless hematuria. He has never had pain crises. His hemoglobin is 14.6 g/dL. Hemoglobin electrophoresis of his sample (lane 3) is shown with control lanes. In each lane, bands closer to the wells (origin, cathode) are, from top to bottom: HbC, HbS, HbF, HbA.
o: Renal papillary necrosis from sickling in the hypoxic medulla
e: Correct. Sickle cell trait (HbA and HbS bands); sickling in the low-Po2 renal medulla causes papillary necrosis.
Wrong. Not suggested by the findings.
q.ch: No crises, no anemia + HbA and HbS bands (figure) → sickle cell trait → medullary sickling → papillary necrosis → hematuria.
q.tr: Electrophoresis order from origin: C, S, F, A ("A Fat Santa Claus" read from the anode).
q.q2: Which of the following best explains his hematuria?

q.s: A 2-year-old girl living in an old rented apartment has irritability, constipation and abdominal pain. She chews on windowsills. Hemoglobin is 9.1 g/dL and MCV is 68 fL. Peripheral smear shows fine blue dots throughout the red cells.
e: Correct. Lead poisoning inhibits both, causing microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling.
cl: living in an old rented apartment
Lead paint in houses built before 1978.
fine blue dots throughout the red cells
q.ch: Child in old housing + pica + colic + microcytic anemia + basophilic stippling → lead poisoning → inhibits ferrochelatase and ALA dehydratase.
q.tr: Lead: LLEEAAD — Lead lines, Encephalopathy, Erythrocyte stippling, Abdominal colic, Anemia, Drops.
q.q2: Which of the following enzymes is inhibited in this patient?

q.s: A 45-year-old man started treatment for latent tuberculosis 4 months ago. He now has fatigue. Hemoglobin is 9.3 g/dL and MCV is 74 fL. Serum iron and ferritin are elevated. Bone marrow aspirate shows erythroid precursors with perinuclear blue granules on Prussian blue stain.
e: Correct. Isoniazid causes B6 deficiency; B6 is the cofactor for ALA synthase. This is sideroblastic anemia.
cl: Serum iron and ferritin are elevated
perinuclear blue granules on Prussian blue stain
q.ch: Isoniazid → B6 deficiency → ALA synthase cannot work → ringed sideroblasts, high iron → pyridoxine.
q.tr: INH depletes B6 → neuropathy and sideroblastic anemia.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

q.s: A 64-year-old woman with vitiligo has numbness of her feet and unsteadiness in the dark. She has decreased vibration and position sense in her legs, a positive Romberg sign and brisk knee reflexes with extensor plantar responses. Hemoglobin is 8.8 g/dL with an MCV of 121 fL. Neutrophils have 6 nuclear lobes.
o: Elevated homocysteine with normal methylmalonic acid
e: Correct. Vitamin B12 deficiency (here likely pernicious anemia) raises both.
cl: brisk knee reflexes with extensor plantar responses
q.ch: Autoimmune background + subacute combined degeneration + megaloblastic anemia → B12 deficiency → high MMA and homocysteine.
q.tr: Neurologic signs + macrocytosis = B12, not folate.
q.q2: Which of the following laboratory findings would confirm the underlying vitamin deficiency?

q.s: A 10-year-old boy has intermittent jaundice and an enlarged spleen. His father had his spleen removed as a teenager. Hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL, MCHC is 37.5 g/dL and reticulocytes are 9%. The smear shows small round red cells without central pallor. The direct antiglobulin test is negative.
e: Correct. Hereditary spherocytosis shows decreased EMA fluorescence (or increased osmotic fragility).
cl: His father had his spleen removed
Autosomal dominant inheritance; splenectomy is treatment.
small round red cells without central pallor
q.ch: Family history + splenomegaly + spherocytes + high MCHC + Coombs negative → hereditary spherocytosis → EMA binding test.
q.tr: Spherocytes + Coombs negative = hereditary spherocytosis; Coombs positive = AIHA.
q.q2: Which of the following tests would best confirm the diagnosis?

q.s: A 28-year-old man from Greece develops dark urine and back pain 3 days after starting primaquine for malaria prophylaxis. Hemoglobin falls from 14.2 to 9.6 g/dL. The smear shows red cells with semicircular defects at the edge.
e: Correct. G6PD deficiency: oxidant stress denatures hemoglobin; splenic removal leaves bite cells.
q.ch: Mediterranean man + oxidant drug → hemolysis with bite cells → G6PD deficiency → Heinz bodies.
q.tr: "Stress makes me eat bites of fava beans with Heinz ketchup."
q.q2: Which of the following inclusions would be seen with a supravital stain?

q.s: A 33-year-old woman has fatigue, dark morning urine and abdominal pain. She has hepatomegaly and ascites. Hemoglobin is 8.4 g/dL, WBC count is 2,900/mm³ and platelets are 88,000/mm³. LDH is high and haptoglobin is undetectable. The direct antiglobulin test is negative. Doppler ultrasound shows hepatic vein thrombosis.
e: Correct. PNH: complement-mediated hemolysis from loss of CD55/CD59; eculizumab blocks C5.
cl: WBC count is 2,900/mm³ and platelets are 88,000/mm³
q.ch: Coombs-negative intravascular hemolysis + pancytopenia + Budd-Chiari → PNH (PIGA, CD55/59 loss) → eculizumab.
q.tr: PNH triad: hemolysis, pancytopenia, thrombosis.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate targeted treatment?

q.s: A 70-year-old man with chronic lymphocytic leukemia has worsening fatigue and jaundice. Hemoglobin is 7.6 g/dL with reticulocytes of 11%. The smear shows spherocytes. The direct antiglobulin test is positive for IgG and negative for complement.
e: Correct. Warm AIHA (IgG, extravascular) is treated with steroids, then rituximab or splenectomy.
cl: positive for IgG and negative for complement
q.ch: CLL + spherocytes + IgG-positive Coombs → warm AIHA → glucocorticoids.
q.tr: "Warm weather is Good" (IgG); cold is IgM + complement.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

q.s: A 19-year-old college student has a dry cough and low-grade fever for 2 weeks. Chest x-ray shows patchy interstitial infiltrates. When she goes outside in winter, her fingertips turn blue and painful. A blood sample clumps visibly when cooled.
e: Correct. Cold agglutinin disease after Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection.
cl: dry cough and low-grade fever for 2 weeks
q.ch: Walking pneumonia + cold-induced acrocyanosis + agglutination when cooled → cold AIHA (IgM + complement) from Mycoplasma.
q.tr: Cold AIHA: Mycoplasma, mono, CLL.
q.q2: Which antibody type is most likely responsible for her hematologic findings?

q.s: A 26-year-old woman develops fatigue, gum bleeding and recurrent infections. She was treated with chloramphenicol for a severe infection 2 months ago. Hemoglobin is 7.2 g/dL, WBC count is 1,400/mm³, platelets are 18,000/mm³ and reticulocytes are 0.2%. No blasts are seen.
e: Correct. Aplastic anemia from drug-induced stem cell injury.
cl: Hemoglobin is 7.2 g/dL, WBC count is 1,400/mm³, platelets are 18,000/mm³
q.ch: Drug exposure + pancytopenia + low reticulocytes, no blasts → aplastic anemia → fatty, hypocellular marrow.
q.tr: Aplastic anemia: empty marrow, normal-looking cells.
q.q2: Which of the following is most likely to be seen on bone marrow biopsy?

q.s: A 58-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has fatigue. Hemoglobin is 10.1 g/dL with an MCV of 82 fL. Serum iron is low, TIBC is low and ferritin is elevated. CRP is high.
e: Wrong. Would cause high TIBC and low ferritin.
Correct. Anemia of chronic disease: IL-6 raises hepcidin, trapping iron in macrophages.
cl: TIBC is low and ferritin is elevated
q.ch: Chronic inflammation + low iron, low TIBC, high ferritin → anemia of chronic disease → hepcidin.
q.tr: Iron deficiency: TIBC up, ferritin down. Chronic disease: both reversed.
q.q2: Which of the following best explains her anemia?

q.s: A 6-year-old boy has a swollen, painful left knee after falling off his bicycle. He has had prolonged bleeding after a tooth extraction. Platelet count, bleeding time and PT are normal; PTT is prolonged and corrects with mixing. His family pedigree is shown; the arrow marks the patient.
e: Correct. Hemophilia A: X-linked recessive (affected males through carrier females), hemarthrosis, isolated prolonged PTT.
Wrong. Mostly autosomal dominant; prolonged bleeding time.
cl: prolonged bleeding after a tooth extraction
PTT is prolonged and corrects with mixing
bleeding time and PT are normal
Platelets and extrinsic pathway are normal.
q.ch: Boy + hemarthrosis + isolated prolonged PTT that corrects + X-linked pedigree (affected uncle, carrier mother) → hemophilia A → factor VIII.
q.tr: Hemophilia A "Ate" (eight); B = IX; both X-linked. C = XI, autosomal recessive.
q.q2: Which factor is most likely deficient?

q.s: A 17-year-old girl has heavy menstrual bleeding since menarche and frequent nosebleeds. Her father bruises easily. Platelet count and PT are normal. Bleeding time is prolonged and PTT is mildly prolonged. Platelet agglutination with ristocetin is reduced and corrects when normal plasma is added.
e: Correct. von Willebrand disease: releases stored vWF and factor VIII from endothelial cells.
cl: heavy menstrual bleeding since menarche and frequent nosebleeds
corrects when normal plasma is added
q.ch: Mucosal bleeding + AD inheritance + long bleeding time + mildly long PTT + ristocetin defect corrected by plasma → vWD → desmopressin.
q.tr: Ristocetin defect that corrects with plasma = vWD; does not correct = Bernard-Soulier.
q.q2: Which of the following is the best treatment before a planned dental extraction?

q.s: A 5-year-old boy has new petechiae and bruising 2 weeks after a viral upper respiratory infection. He is otherwise well, with no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. Hemoglobin and WBC count are normal. Platelet count is 9,000/mm³. The smear shows large platelets and no other abnormal cells.
o: Antibodies against GpIIb/IIIa leading to splenic destruction
Decreased platelet production from marrow infiltration
e: Correct. Immune thrombocytopenia, commonly after a viral illness in children.
Wrong. Other lines are normal and no blasts are seen.
cl: 2 weeks after a viral upper respiratory infection
Hemoglobin and WBC count are normal
q.ch: Child + recent virus + isolated severe thrombocytopenia + otherwise normal → ITP → anti-GpIIb/IIIa antibodies.
q.tr: Isolated thrombocytopenia in a well child after a virus = ITP.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely mechanism?

q.s: A 34-year-old woman is brought in confused with a fever of 38.6°C. She has petechiae on her legs. Her laboratory results are shown.
e: Correct. TTP: ADAMTS13 deficiency leaves large vWF multimers; plasma exchange (with steroids, rituximab).
q.ch: Fever + neurologic changes + MAHA (schistocytes, high LDH) + thrombocytopenia + AKI with normal PT/PTT (table) → TTP → plasma exchange.
q.tr: Normal PT/PTT separates TTP/HUS from DIC.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

q.s: A 3-year-old boy had bloody diarrhea after a petting zoo visit 6 days ago. He is now pale, lethargic and passing little urine. Hemoglobin is 8.2 g/dL, platelets are 42,000/mm³ and creatinine is 2.8 mg/dL. The smear shows helmet-shaped red cell fragments. PT and PTT are normal.
o: Supportive care, including dialysis if needed
e: Correct. HUS from Shiga toxin–producing E. coli O157:H7.
cl: bloody diarrhea after a petting zoo visit
q.ch: Child + bloody diarrhea + MAHA + thrombocytopenia + AKI → HUS (Shiga toxin) → supportive care.
q.tr: HUS = triad + bloody diarrhea; TTP = triad + fever + neurologic symptoms.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

q.s: A 41-year-old man has gum bleeding and easy bruising for 1 week. He is oozing from his venipuncture sites. Hemoglobin is 9 g/dL, WBC count is 32,000/mm³ and platelets are 21,000/mm³. PT and PTT are prolonged, fibrinogen is low and D-dimer is very high. Bone marrow shows many abnormal promyelocytes containing bundles of rod-shaped inclusions.
e: Correct. APL with t(15;17) PML-RARα; ATRA (and arsenic) induce differentiation. DIC is a common presentation.
cl: fibrinogen is low and D-dimer is very high
q.ch: DIC + abnormal promyelocytes with Auer rods → APL, t(15;17) → all-trans retinoic acid.
q.tr: APL is the leukemia that presents with DIC and is treated with vitamin A.
q.q2: Which of the following drugs targets the underlying molecular defect?

q.s: A 62-year-old man is started on unfractionated heparin after hip replacement. His platelet counts over the following days are shown. On day 8 his left leg becomes swollen; ultrasound shows a deep vein thrombosis.
e: Correct. HIT type 2: a >50% fall 5–10 days after heparin with thrombosis; use a direct thrombin inhibitor (or fondaparinux).
Wrong. Risk of skin necrosis; not alone in acute HIT.
Wrong. Type 1 is mild and in the first 2 days.
q.ch: Heparin + platelets fall >50% after day 5 (figure) + new thrombosis → HIT type 2 (anti-PF4/heparin IgG) → stop heparin, start argatroban.
q.tr: HIT: platelets go down, clots go up.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

q.s: A 29-year-old woman has her second deep vein thrombosis. Her first occurred while taking oral contraceptives. Her mother had a pulmonary embolism at 40. PT and PTT are normal. In a clotting assay, adding activated protein C fails to prolong her PTT normally.
o: Mutation in the 3′ untranslated region of prothrombin
e: Wrong. Prolonged PTT, not APC resistance.
Wrong. APC added in the test would still work.
Wrong. Prothrombin G20210A; increases prothrombin levels.
Correct. Factor V Leiden resists inactivation by activated protein C.
cl: Her mother had a pulmonary embolism at 40
adding activated protein C fails to prolong her PTT normally
q.ch: Recurrent VTE + family history + APC resistance → factor V Leiden (Arg506Gln).
q.tr: APC resistance = factor V Leiden, the most common inherited thrombophilia.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely molecular defect?

q.s: A 50-year-old woman is started on warfarin alone for a new deep vein thrombosis. On day 3 she develops painful purple patches on her thighs and abdomen that become black and necrotic.
o: Early depletion of protein C before procoagulant factors fall
e: Correct. Protein C has a short half-life; a transient hypercoagulable state causes microthrombi and skin necrosis, especially with protein C deficiency.
cl: painful purple patches on her thighs and abdomen
Fatty areas typical of warfarin necrosis.
q.ch: Warfarin without bridging → protein C falls first → transient hypercoagulability → skin necrosis.
q.tr: Bridge with heparin until warfarin is therapeutic.
q.q2: Which of the following best explains this complication?

q.s: A 63-year-old woman receives a unit of fresh frozen plasma before a procedure. Within 3 hours she develops fever, severe dyspnea and hypotension. Oxygen saturation is 82%. Chest x-ray shows new bilateral infiltrates. Jugular venous pressure is normal and BNP is not elevated.
e: Wrong. Hypertension, high JVP, high BNP.
Correct. TRALI: noncardiogenic pulmonary edema with hypotension within 6 hours.
cl: Jugular venous pressure is normal and BNP is not elevated
q.ch: Plasma transfusion → hypoxia + hypotension + bilateral infiltrates without volume overload → TRALI.
q.tr: TRALI = hypotension, normal BNP; TACO = hypertension, high BNP.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: A 23-year-old woman has a painless neck mass and night sweats for 2 months. Chest x-ray shows a mediastinal mass. Biopsy of a cervical node shows bands of collagen dividing the node into nodules, with scattered large cells with bilobed nuclei and prominent nucleoli.
e: Correct. Reed-Sternberg cells in nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma.
cl: Young adult peak of the bimodal distribution.
bands of collagen dividing the node into nodules
q.ch: Young woman + B symptoms + mediastinal mass + collagen bands + RS cells → nodular sclerosis Hodgkin → CD15+/CD30+.
q.tr: "2 owl eyes × 15 = 30."
q.q2: The large cells are most likely positive for which markers?

q.s: A 14-year-old boy has a rapidly enlarging abdominal mass and bowel obstruction over 3 weeks. Biopsy shows sheets of medium-sized lymphocytes with a very high proliferation rate and scattered pale macrophages containing debris, giving a "starry sky" appearance.
q.ch: Adolescent + fast-growing abdominal mass + starry sky → Burkitt → t(8;14) c-myc.
q.tr: Endemic Burkitt (Africa) = jaw; sporadic = abdomen/pelvis.
q.q2: Which gene is overexpressed due to a chromosomal translocation in this tumor?

q.s: A 61-year-old woman has had painless swelling of lymph nodes in her neck and groin that has come and gone for 3 years. She feels well. Node biopsy shows closely packed follicles of small cleaved cells throughout the node.
o: Overexpression of an inhibitor of apoptosis from t(14;18)
Overexpression of c-myc driving rapid proliferation
e: Correct. Follicular lymphoma: BCL-2 blocks apoptosis, so cells accumulate slowly (indolent).
cl: has come and gone for 3 years
q.ch: Older adult + painless waxing and waning nodes + follicular pattern → follicular lymphoma → t(14;18) BCL-2.
q.tr: BCL-2 = "Big Cell Lives 2 long" — cells don't die.
q.q2: Which of the following best explains the behavior of this tumor?

q.s: A 71-year-old man has back pain and fatigue. His laboratory results are shown. A skull x-ray shows multiple round, punched-out lesions.
e: Correct. Multiple myeloma with CRAB features; the dipstick misses light chains (Bence Jones protein).
q.ch: Hypercalcemia + renal failure + anemia + bone lesions (CRAB) + high globulin gap + light chain proteinuria missed by dipstick (table) → multiple myeloma → >10% clonal plasma cells.
q.tr: A negative dipstick with heavy urine protein = light chains.
q.q2: Which of the following is most likely to be found on bone marrow biopsy?

q.s: A 69-year-old man has headaches, blurred vision, recurrent nosebleeds and numbness in his feet. He has lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. Funduscopy shows dilated, segmented retinal veins. Calcium and creatinine are normal and skeletal survey shows no lytic lesions.
e: Correct. Waldenström macroglobulinemia: large IgM causes hyperviscosity.
q.ch: Hyperviscosity + neuropathy + lymphadenopathy, HSM + no CRAB → Waldenström → IgM spike.
q.tr: IgM is the largest Ig ("macro"), so it thickens the blood.
q.q2: Serum protein electrophoresis is most likely to show a monoclonal spike of which immunoglobulin?

q.s: A 4-year-old boy with Down syndrome has fever, pallor, bone pain and bruising for 3 weeks. He has hepatosplenomegaly. Hemoglobin is 6.8 g/dL, platelets are 22,000/mm³ and WBC count is 48,000/mm³ with many blasts. Blasts are myeloperoxidase-negative, TdT-positive and CD10-positive.
e: Wrong. Not the classic sanctuary sites.
Correct. ALL spreads to the CNS and testes; prophylaxis and evaluation are needed.
q.ch: Child with Down syndrome + marrow failure + TdT+, CD10+ blasts → B-ALL → CNS and testicular involvement.
q.tr: ALL: TdT+ ("To da T and B precursors"), most common childhood cancer.
q.q2: Which of the following sites should be evaluated because the disease often spreads there?

q.s: A 74-year-old man has lymphocytosis of 62,000/mm³ found on routine blood testing. He feels well and has mild lymphadenopathy. The smear shows small mature lymphocytes and many crushed cells. Flow cytometry shows a B-cell population positive for CD5, CD20 and CD23.
e: Correct. CLL is associated with warm AIHA (and cold AIHA), hypogammaglobulinemia and Richter transformation.
cl: Most common adult leukemia in older adults.
q.ch: Older adult + lymphocytosis + smudge cells + CD5+/CD23+ B cells → CLL → autoimmune hemolysis.
q.tr: CLL = Crushed Little Lymphocytes.
q.q2: Which complication is this patient at increased risk for?

q.s: A 52-year-old man has fatigue, left upper quadrant fullness and recurrent infections. The spleen extends to the pelvis. There is no lymphadenopathy. Hemoglobin is 9.1 g/dL, WBC count is 2,100/mm³ and platelets are 64,000/mm³. Bone marrow aspiration yields no material. Circulating lymphocytes have fine cytoplasmic projections and stain for tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase.
e: Correct. Hairy cell leukemia responds to purine analogs (cladribine, pentostatin).
cl: The spleen extends to the pelvis
Bone marrow aspiration yields no material
q.ch: Middle-aged man + massive spleen + pancytopenia + dry tap + TRAP+ hairy cells → hairy cell leukemia → cladribine.
q.tr: "TRAPped in a hairy situation"; BRAF mutation.
q.q2: Which of the following drugs is first-line therapy?

q.s: A 58-year-old woman has fatigue, early satiety and an enlarged spleen. Her laboratory results are shown.
e: Correct. CML (BCR-ABL, t[9;22]); a tyrosine kinase inhibitor.
Wrong. A leukemoid reaction has a high LAP score and no basophilia.
cl: early satiety and an enlarged spleen
Median age of CML is in the 60s.
q.ch: Very high WBC with all stages of granulocytes + basophilia + low LAP score (table) + splenomegaly → CML → imatinib.
q.tr: Low LAP + basophils = CML; high LAP = leukemoid reaction.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

q.s: A 60-year-old man has headaches, itching after hot showers and episodes of burning pain and redness in his feet. His face is ruddy and the spleen is palpable. Hemoglobin is 19.8 g/dL, WBC count is 13,500/mm³ and platelets are 590,000/mm³. Oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Serum erythropoietin is low.
e: Correct. Polycythemia vera: increased RBCs, WBCs and platelets with low EPO.
cl: burning pain and redness in his feet
q.ch: Panmyelosis + aquagenic pruritus + erythromelalgia + normal O2 + low EPO → polycythemia vera → JAK2 V617F.
q.tr: PV: EPO low (feedback); secondary polycythemia: EPO high.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely mutation?

q.s: A 72-year-old man has fatigue, weight loss and a massively enlarged spleen. Hemoglobin is 8.6 g/dL. The smear shows teardrop-shaped red cells and nucleated red cells with immature granulocytes. Bone marrow aspiration yields no material, and biopsy shows dense reticulin and collagen fibrosis.
e: Correct. Primary myelofibrosis: TGF-β stimulates fibroblasts.
cl: nucleated red cells with immature granulocytes
q.ch: Massive splenomegaly + teardrop cells + leukoerythroblastic smear + dry tap with fibrosis → myelofibrosis → megakaryocyte TGF-β.
q.tr: "Bone marrow cries because it's fibrosed."
q.q2: Which of the following mediators drives the bone marrow changes?

q.s: A 2-year-old boy has a scaly, red rash on his scalp, recurrent ear discharge and a tender swelling over the skull. Skull x-ray shows a punched-out lytic lesion. Biopsy shows sheets of cells with folded, grooved nuclei that are positive for S-100 and CD1a. Electron microscopy shows rod-shaped cytoplasmic granules.
e: Correct. Langerhans cell histiocytosis: Birbeck granules ("tennis rackets"); CD207+.
cl: scaly, red rash on his scalp
q.ch: Child + lytic skull lesion + rash + otitis + S-100/CD1a+ cells with Birbeck granules → Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
q.tr: LCH: CD1a, CD207 (langerin), Birbeck "tennis racket" granules.
q.q2: Which normal cell type do these tumor cells most resemble?

q.s: A 30-year-old man with bulky diffuse large B-cell lymphoma starts chemotherapy. Twenty-four hours later he has muscle cramps and palpitations, and urine output falls. ECG shows peaked T waves. Potassium is 6.9 mEq/L, phosphate is 8.8 mg/dL, calcium is 6.8 mg/dL and uric acid is 14 mg/dL.
e: Wrong. Not recommended; can worsen calcium phosphate precipitation.
Wrong. Prevents new uric acid formation; does not break down existing urate.
Correct. Recombinant uricase converts uric acid to allantoin in tumor lysis syndrome.
cl: Acute kidney injury from urate and phosphate.
q.ch: Chemo for bulky lymphoma → hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, hyperuricemia, AKI → TLS → rasburicase.
q.tr: "BreaK the CUP": ↑K, ↓Ca, ↑Uric acid, ↑PO4.
q.q2: Which of the following drugs would rapidly lower his uric acid by converting it to a soluble metabolite?

q.s: A 55-year-old woman completed chemotherapy for breast cancer 1 year ago. She now has progressive dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea and leg edema. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 30%. Her regimen included a drug that intercalates into DNA and generates free radicals.
e: Correct. An iron chelator that protects against anthracycline (doxorubicin) cardiotoxicity.
cl: dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 30%
intercalates into DNA and generates free radicals
q.ch: Anthracycline (doxorubicin) → free radical myocardial injury → dilated cardiomyopathy → dexrazoxane prevents.
q.tr: Doxorubicin: irreversible; trastuzumab: often reversible.
q.q2: Which agent, if given during chemotherapy, might have prevented this complication?

q.s: A 45-year-old woman with granulomatosis with polyangiitis is treated with an alkylating agent that requires activation in the liver. Three weeks later she has dysuria and gross hematuria. Urine culture is negative.
e: Correct. Binds acrolein, the bladder-toxic metabolite of cyclophosphamide.
q.ch: Cyclophosphamide → acrolein in urine → hemorrhagic cystitis → mesna prevents.
q.tr: Cyclophosphamide = CYstitis.
q.q2: Which drug should have been given with the alkylating agent to prevent this?

q.s: A 27-year-old woman who is Rh-negative delivers her second child at home without prenatal care. Her first child, who is Rh-positive, was born 2 years ago, and she received no medications at that time. The newborn is pale and markedly edematous with ascites and hepatosplenomegaly. The direct antiglobulin test on the infant's red cells is positive.
o: Delivering the first child by cesarean section
Anti-D immune globulin to the mother during and after her first pregnancy
e: Wrong. Treats jaundice, does not prevent sensitization.
Correct. It prevents maternal anti-D IgG formation that causes Rh hemolytic disease in later pregnancies.
q.k: Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn
cl: Sensitization happens in the first pregnancy; disease appears in later ones.
received no medications at that time
direct antiglobulin test on the infant's red cells is positive
q.ch: Rh-negative mother + Rh-positive first child without prophylaxis → maternal anti-D IgG → crosses placenta in the second pregnancy → hydrops fetalis.
q.tr: Rh disease: second pregnancy, severe; ABO disease: first pregnancy, mild.
q.q2: Which of the following would most likely have prevented this outcome?

q.s: A 66-year-old man has a serum protein electrophoresis done because of an elevated total protein on routine testing. It shows a monoclonal IgG spike of 1.1 g/dL. He has no symptoms. Hemoglobin, calcium and creatinine are normal, and a skeletal survey shows no lesions. Bone marrow biopsy shows 5% clonal plasma cells.
o: Reassure and discharge with no follow-up
e: Correct. MGUS: no CRAB, <10% plasma cells, M spike <3 g/dL; about 1–2% per year progress to myeloma.
cl: Hemoglobin, calcium and creatinine are normal
q.ch: Small M spike + no CRAB + <10% plasma cells → MGUS → monitor for progression.
q.tr: MGUS → myeloma at about 1% per year.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
